paragraphs: In the preceding papers, my fellow citizens, I have tried to show you clearly and convincingly how important the Union is to your political safety and happiness. I have set out for you a tangle of dangers you would face if you let the sacred knot that binds the people of America together be cut or dissolved by ambition or avarice, by jealousy or misrepresentation. In the remainder of the inquiry that I propose to take with you, the truths I mean to impress on you will be confirmed further by facts and arguments not yet noticed. The road ahead may sometimes seem tedious or irksome. If it does, remember that you are searching for information on the most momentous subject that can occupy a free people; that the ground you must cross is itself broad; and that sophistry has needlessly made the journey harder by planting mazes along the way. My aim will be to clear the obstacles from your path as briefly as I can without sacrificing usefulness to speed.

Following the plan I have laid down for discussing the subject, the next point to examine is the "insufficiency of the present Confederation to the preservation of the Union." Someone may ask what need there is to reason or offer proof for a position that nobody disputes or doubts, that the understanding and feelings of every class of men accept, and that the opponents of the new Constitution admit in substance as readily as its friends. It must truly be acknowledged that, however they differ in other respects, they generally seem to agree in this view at least: our national system has serious imperfections, and something must be done to rescue us from impending anarchy. The facts behind this opinion are no longer matters for speculation. They have forced themselves on the feelings of the people at large. They have also wrung a reluctant admission from the very people whose mistaken policy did most to bring us to our present extremity. The admission is that these defects in the scheme of our federal government are real, defects which the intelligent friends of the Union have long pointed out and regretted.

We may fairly say that we have almost reached the last stage of national humiliation. There is scarcely anything that can wound the pride or degrade the character of an independent nation that we do not suffer. Are there engagements that every tie respected among men binds us to keep? They are constantly and shamelessly violated. Do we owe debts to foreigners and to our own citizens, contracted in a time of imminent peril to preserve our political existence? They remain without any proper or satisfactory provision for payment. Does a foreign power hold valuable territories and important posts that, by express stipulation, ought long ago to have been surrendered? It still keeps them, to the injury of our interests as much as of our rights. Are we in a position to resent or repel the aggression? We have neither troops, nor treasury, nor government.(1) Are we even in a position to protest with dignity? First, the just charges against our own good faith under the same treaty would have to be cleared away. Are we entitled by nature and by compact to a free share in the navigation of the Mississippi? Spain shuts us out of it. Is public credit an indispensable resource in time of public danger? We seem to have given up its cause as desperate and beyond recovery. Is commerce important to national wealth? Ours has sunk to its lowest point. Is respectability in the eyes of foreign powers a safeguard against foreign encroachments? The impotence of our government keeps them from even negotiating with us. Our ambassadors abroad are the mere pageants of a mock sovereignty. Is a violent and unnatural fall in the value of land a symptom of national distress? In most parts of the country, improved land sells for much less than the quantity of wasteland on the market can explain. The only full explanation is the lack of private and public confidence, which is alarmingly widespread among all ranks and which tends directly to lower the value of property of every kind. Is private credit the friend and patron of industry? The most useful kind, the kind that concerns borrowing and lending, has shrunk to the narrowest limits, and this comes still more from a belief that lending is unsafe than from a scarcity of money. I will cut short a list of particulars that can give neither pleasure nor instruction. We may ask in general: what sign of national disorder, poverty, and insignificance could strike a community as richly blessed with natural advantages as ours that is not already part of the dark catalogue of our public misfortunes?

We have been brought to this melancholy situation by the very maxims and counsels that now try to scare us away from adopting the proposed Constitution. Not content with leading us to the brink of a precipice, they seem determined to push us into the abyss below. Here, my countrymen, let us take a firm stand for our safety, our tranquillity, our dignity, and our reputation, moved by every motive that ought to move an enlightened people. Let us at last break the fatal spell that has too long drawn us away from the paths of happiness and prosperity.

It is true, as I have observed before, that facts too stubborn to resist have produced a kind of general agreement with the abstract proposition that our national system has serious defects. But the old adversaries of federal measures spoil the usefulness of this concession by strenuously opposing a remedy built on the only principles that can give it a chance of success. They admit that the government of the United States has no energy, yet they argue against giving it the powers needed to supply that energy. They still seem to aim at things that contradict each other and cannot be reconciled: an increase of federal authority with no decrease of State authority; sovereignty in the Union with complete independence in its members. They still, in short, seem to cherish with blind devotion the political monster of an imperium in imperio. For this reason a full account of the principal defects of the Confederation is necessary. It will show that the evils we suffer do not come from minor or partial imperfections. They come from fundamental errors in the structure of the building, and these cannot be corrected without changing the first principles and main pillars of the fabric.

The great and radical vice in the construction of the existing Confederation is the principle of LEGISLATION for STATES or GOVERNMENTS, in their CORPORATE or COLLECTIVE CAPACITIES, as distinguished from the INDIVIDUALS of which they consist. This principle does not run through all the powers delegated to the Union, but it pervades and governs those on which the effectiveness of the rest depends. Except for the rule of appointment, the United States has unlimited discretion to make requisitions, or formal requests, for men and money. But it has no authority to raise either through regulations that reach the individual citizens of America. The consequence is that in theory the resolutions of the United States on these subjects are laws, constitutionally binding on the members of the Union, but in practice they are mere recommendations that the States may observe or disregard as they please.

It is a singular instance of the capriciousness of the human mind that, after all that experience has taught us on this point, some men still object to the new Constitution because it departs from a principle that has proved the bane of the old one. That principle is plainly incompatible, in itself, with the very idea of GOVERNMENT. If it is to be carried out at all, it must put the violent and bloody agency of the sword in place of the mild influence of the civil authority.

There is nothing absurd or impracticable in a league or alliance between independent nations for certain defined purposes. Such a league would be set out in a treaty that precisely states the purposes and regulates every detail of time, place, circumstance, and quantity, leaves nothing to later discretion, and relies for its execution on the good faith of the parties. Compacts of this kind exist among all civilized nations. They are subject to the usual ups and downs of peace and war, of observance and non-observance, as the interests or passions of the contracting powers dictate. In the early part of this century Europe was seized by an epidemic rage for compacts of this kind, and the politicians of the day fondly hoped they would bring benefits that were never realized. To establish the balance of power and the peace of that part of the world, every resource of negotiation was exhausted, and triple and quadruple alliances were formed. Scarcely had they been formed when they were broken. They taught mankind an instructive but painful lesson: very little dependence can be placed on treaties that have no sanction beyond the obligations of good faith, and that set general considerations of peace and justice against the pull of any immediate interest or passion.

Suppose the individual States of this country are willing to stand in a similar relation to each other and to give up the project of a general DISCRETIONARY SUPERINTENDENCE. The scheme would then indeed be harmful, and it would bring on all the harms listed under the first head. But it would have the merit of being at least consistent and practicable. We would abandon every view toward a confederate government and arrive at a simple alliance, offensive and defensive. We would be placed in a situation where we would be alternately friends and enemies of each other, as our mutual jealousies and rivalries, fed by the intrigues of foreign nations, should direct.

But suppose we are unwilling to be placed in this perilous situation, and still hold to the design of a national government, which is the same as a superintending power under the direction of a common council. Then we must resolve to build into our plan the ingredients that can be considered the characteristic difference between a league and a government. We must extend the authority of the Union to the persons of the citizens, who are the only proper objects of government.

Government implies the power of making laws. It is essential to the idea of a law that it carry a sanction, in other words a penalty or punishment for disobedience. If no penalty is attached to disobedience, the resolutions or commands that pretend to be laws will in fact be nothing more than advice or recommendation. This penalty, whatever it may be, can be inflicted in only two ways: through the courts and ministers of justice, or through military force. That is, it is either the COERCION of the civil authority or the COERCION of arms. The first kind can evidently apply only to individual men. The last kind must of necessity be used against bodies politic, or communities, or States. It is evident that no process of a court can, in the last resort, enforce the observance of the laws against them. Sentences may be pronounced against them for violations of their duty, but those sentences can be carried out only by the sword. In an association where the general authority is confined to the collective bodies of the communities that compose it, every breach of the laws must involve a state of war, and military execution must become the only instrument of civil obedience. Such a state of things surely cannot deserve the name of government, and no prudent man would choose to entrust his happiness to it.

There was a time when we were told not to expect the States to breach the regulations of the federal authority. A sense of common interest, we were told, would govern the conduct of the individual members and produce full compliance with all the constitutional requisitions of the Union. Today this language would sound as wild as a great part of what we now hear from the same quarter will sound once further lessons from experience, that best oracle of wisdom, have reached us. At every time it betrayed ignorance of the true springs of human conduct, and it contradicted the original reasons for establishing civil power. Why was government instituted at all? Because the passions of men will not follow the dictates of reason and justice unless they are constrained. Has it been found that bodies of men act with more rectitude or greater disinterestedness than individuals do? All careful observers of human conduct have inferred the opposite, and the inference rests on obvious reasons. Regard for reputation has less effect when the disgrace of a bad action is shared among many than when it falls on one person alone. A spirit of faction tends to mix its poison into the deliberations of every body of men. It will often carry the persons who make up such a body into improprieties and excesses that they would blush at in a private capacity.

On top of all this, sovereign power by its nature is impatient of control. It disposes those who hold it to look with an evil eye on every outside attempt to restrain or direct its operations. This spirit explains why, in every political association formed on the principle of uniting a number of lesser sovereignties in a common interest, there is a kind of eccentric tendency in the subordinate or inferior orbs. Each makes a perpetual effort to fly off from the common center. This tendency is not hard to account for. It begins in the love of power. Power that is controlled or limited is almost always the rival and enemy of the power that controls or limits it. This simple proposition shows how little reason there is to expect that the persons entrusted with the affairs of the individual members of a confederacy will at all times be ready to carry out the resolutions or decrees of the general authority with perfect good humor and an unbiased regard for the public welfare. The reverse follows from the make-up of human nature.

If, therefore, the measures of the Confederacy cannot be carried out without the intervention of the particular administrations, there is little prospect that they will be carried out at all. The rulers of the individual members will undertake to judge the propriety of the measures themselves, whether or not they have a constitutional right to. They will ask whether what is proposed or required suits their immediate interests or aims, and what momentary conveniences or problems would come with adopting it. All this will be done in a spirit of interested and suspicious scrutiny. It will be done without the knowledge of national circumstances and reasons of state that a right judgment requires, and with a strong preference for local objects that can hardly fail to mislead the decision. The same process must be repeated in every member of which the body is made up. The carrying out of plans framed by the councils of the whole will always depend on the discretion of the ill-informed and prejudiced opinion of each part. Consider those who have watched the proceedings of popular assemblies and seen how hard it often is, even when no outside pressure of circumstances exists, to bring them to harmonious resolutions on important points. They will readily see how impossible it must be to induce a number of such assemblies, deliberating at a distance from each other, at different times, and under different impressions, to cooperate for long in the same views and pursuits.

In our case, the Confederation requires the concurrence of thirteen distinct sovereign wills for the complete execution of every important measure that proceeds from the Union. It has turned out as might have been foreseen. The measures of the Union have not been carried out. The delinquencies of the States have matured step by step to an extreme that has at last stopped all the wheels of the national government and brought them to a dreadful standstill. Congress now scarcely has the means to keep up the forms of administration until the States can find time to agree on a more substantial replacement for the present shadow of a federal government. Things did not reach this desperate extreme at once. The causes I have named at first produced only unequal and disproportionate degrees of compliance with the requisitions of the Union. The greater deficiencies of some States gave the complying States, or the least delinquent, a pretext in their example and a temptation in their own interest. Why should we do more in proportion than those embarked with us on the same political voyage? Why should we agree to bear more than our proper share of the common burden? Human selfishness could not withstand such suggestions, and even speculative men, who looked ahead to remote consequences, could not combat them without hesitation. Each State, yielding to the persuasive voice of immediate interest or convenience, has in turn withdrawn its support, until the frail and tottering edifice seems ready to fall on our heads and crush us beneath its ruins.
